scenes.tts: Back to the thirsty mouse. Its thirst neurons go quiet within a minute. No change in the blood has been detected. So what has changed?
scenes.visual: The mouse at the spout again. The question appears above.
scenes.narration: Back to the thirsty mouse. Its thirst neurons go quiet within a minute. No change in the blood has been detected. So what has changed?

scenes.tts: Researchers recorded subfornical organ neurons in awake mice, using an optical fibre and a calcium indicator.
scenes.visual: A fibre over the subfornical organ; a population of neurons glows green. Label: fibre photometry, population calcium.
scenes.narration: Researchers recorded subfornical organ neurons in awake mice, using an optical fibre and a calcium indicator.

scenes.tts: Picture the neurons and the blood on one time axis. A line marks when water arrives.
scenes.visual: One time axis, labelled schematic. An upper lane for a continuous neural trace; a lower lane for blood sample points. A vertical line: water available.
scenes.narration: Picture the neurons and the blood on one time axis. A line marks when water arrives.

scenes.tts: The neurons' activity starts to fall at the first lick. Within a minute, it is down.
scenes.visual: The upper trace (SFO activity) drops at the first lick and is low within one minute.
scenes.narration: The neurons' activity starts to fall at the first lick. Within a minute, it is down.

scenes.tts: The blood was sampled, not traced. Plasma osmolality was still raised five minutes after water access.
scenes.visual: In the lower lane, separate plasma osmolality samples appear as points with error bars, still high at five minutes. No line is drawn between them. Label: sampled separately.
scenes.narration: The blood was sampled, not traced. Plasma osmolality was still raised five minutes after water access.

scenes.tts: What could turn the neurons down? The sight of water? The licking? Or the water itself?
scenes.visual: Three small panels: a water bottle out of reach, a mouse licking an empty spout, water going into the mouth. Question marks on each.
scenes.narration: What could turn the neurons down? The sight of water? The licking? Or the water itself?

scenes.tts: Seeing water it could not reach did not lower the activity. Licking an empty bottle did not either.
scenes.visual: The first two panels show flat, high traces; each is crossed out.
scenes.narration: Seeing water it could not reach did not lower the activity. Licking an empty bottle did not either.

scenes.tts: So it is something that comes with fluid going in.
scenes.visual: The third panel is highlighted.
scenes.narration: So it is something that comes with fluid going in.

scenes.tts: Drinking concentrated saline lowers it at first, like water. After about a minute, the fall reverses.
scenes.visual: A saline panel: the trace drops, then climbs back after about a minute.
scenes.narration: Drinking concentrated saline lowers it at first, like water. After about a minute, the fall reverses.

scenes.tts: A fast signal counts fluid going in. A slower one reports what the fluid contains.
scenes.visual: Two labels on the saline trace: fast signal, fluid in; slower signal, what it contains.
scenes.narration: A fast signal counts fluid going in. A slower one reports what the fluid contains.

scenes.tts: Next, bypass the mouth. Put water straight into the stomach.
scenes.visual: Schematic: water infused through a tube into the stomach while the fibre records.
scenes.narration: Next, bypass the mouth. Put water straight into the stomach.

scenes.tts: In dehydrated mice, the activity falls in about two minutes. Separate blood measurements found no detectable change in osmolarity, so the response comes first.
scenes.visual: Schematic, labelled schematic. Main panel: the SFO calcium trace in dehydrated mice falls after gut water; label: latency 107 ± 15 s (mean ± SEM), about 2 min. A separate inset, not on the same time points: separate measurements in hydrated mice; blood collection began at 3 min and took about 3 min; no detectable osmolarity change. No plasma point is drawn at 2 min.
scenes.narration: In dehydrated mice, the activity falls in about two minutes. Separate blood measurements found no detectable change in osmolarity, so the response comes first.

scenes.tts: Hypertonic saline in the stomach raises the activity instead.
scenes.visual: A second infusion panel: hypertonic saline into the stomach; the SFO trace rises.
scenes.narration: Hypertonic saline in the stomach raises the activity instead.

scenes.tts: Then researchers used light to hold the neurons active. Now water in the gut no longer brings its usual satiation.
scenes.visual: Light on the fibre keeps the SFO trace high during gut water; a drinking bar stays high. Label: optogenetic activation.
scenes.narration: Then researchers used light to hold the neurons active. Now water in the gut no longer brings its usual satiation.

scenes.tts: Suppose the brain read only the blood. How much would a thirsty animal drink?
scenes.visual: A mouse drinking beside a gut filling with water and a blood gauge that has not yet moved. A question mark.
scenes.narration: Suppose the brain read only the blood. How much would a thirsty animal drink?

scenes.tts: Too much, if it drinks faster than water is absorbed. Water reaches the blood gradually, so a blood-only brain keeps drinking.
scenes.visual: A toy-model panel, labelled illustrative: drinking fast compared with absorption. The gut fills; the blood gauge lags; the drinking counter climbs past the deficit.
scenes.narration: Too much, if it drinks faster than water is absorbed. Water reaches the blood gradually, so a blood-only brain keeps drinking.

scenes.tts: So the estimate must count what is on its way.
scenes.visual: The estimate card returns: the estimate is the blood, corrected for what is on its way. Predicted deficit = current body-water deficit − swallowed water still awaiting absorption. Small label: illustrative model; complete retention, no ongoing losses.
scenes.narration: So the estimate must count what is on its way.

scenes.tts: The brain can also learn. In trained mice, vasopressin neurons dipped when a water bowl arrived, before any drinking.
scenes.visual: A water bowl slides into a cage. A vasopressin-neuron trace dips before the first lick.
scenes.narration: The brain can also learn. In trained mice, vasopressin neurons dipped when a water bowl arrived, before any drinking.

scenes.tts: So feedforward can sense fluid going in, or predict it from a learned cue.
scenes.visual: Two labels: sensed (mouth and gut); predicted (learned cue).
scenes.narration: So feedforward can sense fluid going in, or predict it from a learned cue.

scenes.tts: Keep the limits. This is population calcium, recorded in mice. It is not the feeling of thirst.
scenes.visual: A small caveat card: population calcium, not spikes; mice; not the feeling of thirst.
scenes.narration: Keep the limits. This is population calcium, recorded in mice. It is not the feeling of thirst.

scenes.tts: Feedback reads the blood. Feedforward reads what is coming. The estimate is the blood, corrected for what is on its way.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: feedback reads the blood now; feedforward anticipates from the mouth, the gut and learned cues. The estimate = the blood, corrected for what is on its way.
scenes.narration: Feedback reads the blood. Feedforward reads what is coming. The estimate is the blood, corrected for what is on its way.
